comments.body: I like great movies, and what a story to base one on. But while Nolan's take had some spectacle, my wife and I found the narrative treatment disjointed and weak in many places. My wife and I know the story well but thought someone coming to it without some prep would be confused. Several of the fascinating key characters had almost zero development. Who are these characters and why are they doing what they're doing? I understand the source material is a lot to pack into a three-hour movie. The Odyssey defines "epic" storytelling. Maybe a one-season miniseries would have helped? Nolan's SOP to jarringly shift locations and times pays off at times, but in the Odyssey it added to the narrative confusion, IMO. Still, there was cool stuff to see.

comments.body: I expected to like it, and I didn't. The immaculate armor (never previously worn in battle?) looked like what you pick up at a Halloween store. Smooth, plastic, far beyond the technology of the time. At times I felt transported into a Star Wars movie by the look of some of the armored creatures. It was more of a sketch of the tale than a real telling -- I wondered what people made of it who had never read it in any form. But I suppose they were enjoying the fantasy-tale effects. Many scenes were too long without advancing the story -- especially the final battle with the suitors. I kept waiting for Odysseus to do a martial arts back flip. And I must confess that my mental image of the horse included wheels. Looking at the actors packed inside, my main thought was that they weren't being paid enough, however much it was.

The basic problem with a lot of business-oriented Republicans and tech bros is that they keep trying to run public services "like a business"...while failing to understand why public services work incredibly badly as "businesses" and only work well as "services." In that sense, Ramaswamy is nothing new. 

To pick an obvious example, schools can't run like businesses because the schools don't get to fire their weakest students and don't get to get to dodge the expenses of their high needs students by shoving them out the door. A private school that gets to hand-pick its student body and "advise out" or expel its neediest students is going to get better test scores than a public school -- regardless of what happens in the classroom -- because its business model involves dodging problems. But public services don't work like that. You don't get to just "dodge" expensive health care patients, either.

This is why businessmen tend to make appallingly incompetent political leaders. They have no experience with serving others and only with pushing problems out the door for someone else to handle. Then they are surprised when those same problems come back to them in a different form. Donald Trump is the poster child for this principle, but Ramaswamy seems to be following exactly in his footsteps.

Eliminating forward guidance forces markets to continuously guess the Federal Reserve’s reaction function rather than aligning with its medium-term trajectory. When investors lack clear policy signals, bond yields tend to overreact to isolated economic data prints, spiking volatility and driving up term premiums (the extra yield investors demand for holding long-term debt under high policy uncertainty).

Monetary policy operates primarily through financial conditions—mortgage rates, corporate borrowing yields, and equity valuations—which depend heavily on future rate expectations, not just the current overnight target rate. Clear guidance allows the Fed to tighten or ease financial conditions instantly without waiting for formal FOMC voting cycles. Retracting guidance dilutes the immediate impact of central bank strategy.

But through it all Ma is steady and consistent and guiding. She is not what we’d call a kind or loving parent today - and her lines against the Native Americans still cut deep. She was open-minded in other ways, and was a good mother and provider and did her best to raise her kids in her world under extraordinary circumstances. she is everything to the family and the appreciation and love comes through on every page, and in the TV and Netflix adaptations

comments.name: Karen Norris
comments.body: I loved the whole series as a child, and what impressed me most were all the skills a person had to have to live in a prairie wilderness. Ma knew how to make cheese, soap, sew, cook, garden, milk cows, make straw tick mattresses, and she was a contra-alto, and a schoolteacher. While doing all of this she kept her ears covered, wore her corsets to bed every night, brushed her hair 100 strokes nightly, and wore her sunbonnet religiously. So although she preached against vanity she took care of herself by the standards of the day. She pointed out to Laura one time that her Pa could span her waist with his two hands when they were first married, to which Laura replied, "Well, he can't now, and he seems to like you." Ma smiled (apparently amused) and told Laura not to be saucy. I didn't really feel sorry for Ma because she seemed so incredibly "capable" to me and her corrections to her daughters were appropriate for the time, and served them well. Regarding Laura having to work to support Mary's tuition, I got the impression that Laura really didn't mind doing this because she loved her big sister and mourned her blindness, so I got the impression she was glad to do it. Pa wasn't the best provider in the world, but he was compassionate, and fun, and played the violin. Perhaps their frequent moves occurred because he just kept hoping he would be a "success." at the new location. I still think the books provide a positive and accessible, if incomplete, window into our history.

Indian economy is failing in its most important task, namely, generating meaningful employment for India’s vast young population (age group 15-25). While the overall unemployment is low, a large number of college graduates fail to find stable, salaried positions and end up working in informal sectors.  The frustration among the youth is real. There are other things in this opinion piece that, to various extent, are true.

Mobile connectivity, unified payment system, investments in infrastructure, etc. are very popular too. So, yes, Mr. Modi’s aura of invincibility has been dented. His party may even lose elections. That happens all the time in democracies. And that is good and a very healthy thing. 

The roots of Indian democracy are far too strong. This has been repeatedly demonstrated, most notably, in the defeat of Mrs. Gandhi following the end of her emergency rule.  It is good that the young Indians succeeded. But Indian democracy was in no need of a life boat. It was not drowning, and it wasn’t facing extinction.

Mr. Modi promised clean governance, jobs, and economic transformation. Instead, India has seen increasingly centralized decision-making, questions about the independence of institutions, selective use of investigative agencies against political opponents, and growing reliance on welfare promises after years of criticizing "freebies."

Economic growth has been real, but its benefits have been uneven. It often feels like a quintile economy, rewarding the top fifth far more than the rest. Demonetization imposed enormous hardship while failing to achieve its stated goals, and the abrupt COVID lockdown triggered one of the largest internal migrations in independent India.

comments.name: C Christy
comments.body: Is it possible for the NYT to retire "Chinese competition" as a phrase? Competition implies rival firms fighting for profit in a market. What's described here, dozens of automakers losing money for years, kept alive by state credit and local government stakes, is not competition. It's a state flooding global markets with underpriced product to buy market share and strategic leverage, with losses absorbed as the cost of doing geopolitics. The piece even quotes an industry consultant admitting as much, then reverts to "competition" a paragraph later. Germany's labor rigidity is a real problem and worth the scrutiny this article gives it. But calling this contest symmetrical, as though BYD and Volkswagen are just unequally talented players in the same game, flatters Beijing's strategy by mislabeling it.

comments.name: Lambros Balatsias

comments.name: Charles Michener
comments.body: I don't think the general voting public thinks in terms of who's "moderate,""left-wing" or "democratic socialist" (though "socialist" probably scares a lot of affluent, older Democrats and independents, not to mention anti-Trump Republicans). With all respect to the astuteness in this conversation, I think the political commentariat needs to jettison the old labels and focus on the issues and personal attributes of candidates that actually make a difference in the voting booths. Democrats have been on the losing side in recent decades because they talk too much in abstractions - democracy," "fairness," "equality," "bipartisanship," etc. - and not enough in blunt, down-to-earth language aimed at everyday concerns and fears about the immediate future. As for Israel,  appalled as many may be by the Netanyahu government, I daresay that most Americans don't read Tom Friedman (or Bret Stephens) and have much more pressing things on their mind.

comments.name: Robert Vukovic

It's also time for the working class to abandon any labor union leaders who supported and/or endorsed Trump.

I'm a huge supporter of sticking with the Unions, except when they're sticking it to their rank-and-file membership.

comments.name: Perry J. Greenbaum
comments.body:
I am a Canadian, a liberal, who comes from working-class roots all the way down the line. Yes, I am educated, and classified as middle-class, but still adhere to the way I was raised. 

My sympathies lie with the downtrodden, the working poor, etc. I root for them to have a better life; I vote for politicians here in Canada whose policies will do just that. Aim to make life easier and better economically.

That being said, I am astounded that any working-class family in America would even think of voting for any Republican candidate. The GOP has always, and I have been following politics since Watergate, been the party of big businesss and the wealthy.

The Democratic Party, if it is to win over the working-class, has to move away from Wall Street and toward Main Street. Listen to what your constituents are saying. It's the economy; it's jobs; it's housing: it's groceries; it"s prices at the pumps.

Democratic candidates need to push down on the pedal the coordinated message that most Americans can't afford to live. There is an affordability crisis directly caused by the man sitting in the White House. That the last 18 months have been horrible.

comments.body: I enjoy these opinion columnist panels so much in great part because of how collegial everyone is. I’m aware that each person may come from a different ideological perspective but the calm and respectful and frankly friendly way that they interact and listen to one another gives me a fragile hope and models what is possible in this country.

comments.name: Brad Martin
comments.body:
I think millennials now represent the largest generation and to the extent that generations create voting blocs, here they are. Except the reality is that age and cohort is only part of how people see politics. Just like for my generation, there wasn't a single Vietnam experience but very different experiences depending on class and background. 

Just for me personally, I voted Republican consistently from the time I was old enough to vote and grew old thinking myself a John McCain Republican. I get that he wasn't perfect, but since 2016, I've been a straight-ticket Democratic voter. Not because I agree with everything every Democrat says but because I simply can't abide the awfulness someone like Stephen Miller propounds. I'm not sure what kind of coalition evolves to become something like a decent center, but I'd vote for that, even if the candidate has some kind of leftist label. In saying that, I also understand that I could be pushed into positions I find uncomfortable. I don't and shouldn't always get my way. But some things are intolerable. More of those things come from the right - where I grew up - than from the left.

Why should I vote at all?  

At least in Europe everyone benefits - here we always exclude those with earned income while letting investors off the hook -  carried interest is especially egregious due to their damage they do to the rest of us.

comments.body:
A winning position for any Democrat running for national office is to promise they'll do everything they can to lower the age of Medicare qualification to 50 years old.  

Many unemployed Americans in the age group 50-65 are looking for jobs with medical benefits, but are shut out of the labor market.

Other Americans in this age group who have jobs with medical benefits would like to retire, but can't afford insurance on the private market. They may also be carrying spouses on their insurance plans who also lie within this age group, another incentive to keep working at their current jobs.

Besides directly helping those in the 50-65 demographic, two important by-products of such a change are: (1) jobs would open up as more people have an incentive to retire and (2) co-workers and customers would no longer have to deal with people who are miserable in their current jobs and are only staying on for the medical benefits. 

Win-win-win.

comments.body:
The freedom that MAHA advocates is the freedom to believe that you are special, that statistics don't apply to you and despite evidence and probability, you can get well by doing something different from what doctors recommend.

I understand the pull of magical thinking. After lifetimes of good health, my wife and I, in our late 60s, are beset by issues: arthritis and cardiac for me, extremely rare cancer for her. Our doctors have little or nothing to say on the causes of these things, those are just unknowns. But they know what *on average* gives the longest survival. I'd be lying to say the wish for a magic peptide, or whatever, to just make it all go away hasn't crossed my mind. But we go with the X% chance of Y more years that the doctor offers. To think we are special and that the rules don't apply to us would be no more than selfish egotism.

We seem to be rushing head first toward the types of tragedies that birthed the various food, drug and cosmetic acts of the last century. People, particularly children, had to die back then in order for adequate protections against ‘snake oil’ to be enacted. Amnesia and the profit motive, aided by a malevolent Health Secretary, have lead to an explosion of influencers with unproven products to sell. I’ve seen many ads for a blue pill for male sexual dysfunction that contains 2 actual pharmaceutical products, but at subtherapeutic doses, along with another drug that only works when injected and fourth drug thrown in for no apparent reason, all hawked by gorgeous, scantily clad women. 

We can thank the late Senator, Orrin Hatch, for ensuring that the FDA could not hold supplements to the same safety and efficacy standards that prescription drugs are held to, a legacy that is sure to make us much less healthy.

comments.body:
As s 15 year Key West resident, I applaud and encourage the people who say that they won't come to Key West because of Florida's political climate. I also like those who won't come for any other reason.
Our little island, with its fragile infrastructure needs fewer visitors, not more.

comments.name: John Teets
comments.body: Running stories about Key West by someone who lives here would be a useful tool against simple mistakes. It's the Studios OF Key West, not at, and the Key West Bight is so much non-formerly that it falls under the municipal Key West Bight Management District Board.

comments.name: Grace
comments.body:
Reading some of the comments about the dislike for all of Florida (politics) and commercialism... I get it, but I lived in the Keys in the 70's - 80's... I loved that it felt separate from the rest of the world.. from the ole USA.  On some local tv station they'd show the national weather map and I loved seeing way down, way down the coast of Florida to the sprinkling chain of little islands... The Florida Keys - my home!  "Leave me alone northern world" 

Yes, in some respects it is over run by tourism, T- shirt shops, and cruise ships (Key West)... but when I die I want my ashes spread in the waters flowing under Seven Mile Bridge.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body:
In the mid-80’s I lived in Key West in a rented, furnished apartment behind the home of a true Conch lady who had never in her 60+ years of life been further north than Miami. My rent was $400 a month which I split with my housemate and I covered in one night tending bar. (The other five nights of the week were gravy.)
I wrote (by hand, with ink on paper) my application essays for St. John’s College while living there. When I got accepted my co-workers threw me a goodbye party telling me to “get out while you still can.”

comments.name: BC
comments.body: You should add poets James Merrill and Richard Wilbur to your list of Key West luminaries.

comments.name: Walter Provencher
comments.body:
Of the many Key West literary anecdotes, perhaps my favorite is the midnight punch-up between two poetry heavyweights, Robert Frost and Wallace Stevens.  It all started after a few drinks.
Stevens teased, 'The trouble with you, Robert, is that you write about subjects.'  Frost retorted:  'The trouble with you, Wallace, is that you write about--bric-a-brac.'  Fisty-cuffs ensured, with Stevens decking Frost, obviously a bit out of his weight class.  Later, Stevens made up, sending Frost a new book, inscribing it, 'To Robert... here's some more bric-a-brac.'

Alcohol and mankind have been partners for tens of thousands of years.

I'm turning/have turned into a non-drinker. Why? Small amounts of alcohol give me a pounding headache and wake me up to 1am. It isn't a logic decision about whether alcohol is good or bad for my health. It's a feeling, like stubbing your toe. It hurts, so stop.

I'm a boomer.  I suspect a major reason for the reduction in alcohol consumption boils down to a lot of people getting old and no longer wanting to stub their toes.

comments.name: Mary
comments.body:
I gave up drinking alcohol not for health reasons, but just to see what my life would look like without drinking. My experience was very different than when I just drank less often. It was a strict no alcohol thing I was trying. It was weird at first, people thought I was some kind of prohibitionist, someone morally against drinking, and nothing could be further from the truth. 

I remember when smoking was also a social glue, taking a smoking break at work with coworkers, having a cigarette to relax, etc was a social norm. I felt a bit left out of this shared comradery being a non-smoker. But then, in a relatively short amount of time, cigarette smoking, as a social bonding activity just ended, everywhere.

After a few months of no alcohol in my life, my thinking about it changed, I began to see drinking alcohol as an advertising driven sales pitch that was not allowing people to feel okay with saying no. I'm totally in support of those having a drink, just don't get on my case for having a non-alcoholic drink. 

Actually, I feel so much better, I can feel a bit more awkward socially sometimes, but also more authentic somehow. I am more honest and if I feel a bit awkward, so what. I'm a grownup. I've grown emotionally in significant ways since I stopped drinking. Before, I would have let the drink just wave me through it.

comments.name: Maybe

I worry more about video games and phones like the one I am typing on right now as being more of a drain on social life, especially for younger people, than I do about the decrease in alcohol consumption. Go for a walk and say hello to your neighbors. Find a hobby. Many organizations not centered around alcohol would love to see you attend their next event, give it a try.

Demand Side:
The consumers for these products are being drawn in by large IT tech firms with following through low cost to free platforms (social media, email service etc.), regardless of like or dislike by consumers.    There are of course smaller market segments with more customized end users.  The demand curve is nearly flat due to this lopsidedness.

Supply side:
The supply side of the product is driven by innovation with faster computing, learning models, large volumes of data etc.
The product generators are offering to produce more AI widgets at lower price levels.  As result, whatever the supply curve, it is flattening.

Pricing is set by intersection of the supply and demand curves.   When the curves are flat, they will not meet and hence the rampant speculation as in bubbles.  When there is true price discovery through curve intersection, there will be a bust.

It’s fascinating to read comments from people who believe that meaningful oversight and accountability for a police department with a long and sordid history of corruption, racism, extrajudicial punishment, and wrongful killings somehow amount to “defunding the police.” I get that some frightened people would prefer to live in a police state, but that is not what most New Yorkers want.

What we want are police officers who respect the communities they serve and perform their duties with honor and integrity. Since the NYPD’s leadership has repeatedly demonstrated that it is unwilling or unable to achieve that through effective training, supervision, and internal discipline, it falls to the community, through the CCRB, to hold individual officers accountable and force the department’s management to confront systemic misconduct.

I wish we could ask Amadou Diallo what he thinks about police reform. But he was killed in a hail of 41 gunshots by four white NYPD officers after reaching for his wallet in the vestibule of his own building. The officers were acquitted, and the department escaped meaningful accountability. 

Mr. Diallo’s killing was not an isolated aberration. It was one of many cases in which innocent civilians were killed by NYPD officers, no one was held responsible, and the culture of the department remained fundamentally unchanged.

Why should expecting accountability from those entrusted with policing NYC be viewed as anti-police rather than pro-accountability?

comments.name: Bill

The fundamental weakness of the Civilian Complaint Review Board is embedded in its very structure. The CCRB can investigate allegations, substantiate misconduct, and recommend discipline, but it cannot impose punishment. The NYPD routinely rejects the board’s recommendations without consequence, leaving police brass to decide whether CCRB findings will be taken seriously or simply ignored. It is the proverbial fox guarding the henhouse.

New Yorkers can file complaints, investigators can assemble evidence, and board members can reach findings, but the process ultimately ends at the very department being scrutinized.

The CCRB is less an independent accountability mechanism than the carefully constructed appearance of one. It gives New Yorkers a formal place to report misconduct and allows city officials to point to the existence of civilian review, while the NYPD remains free to reject its conclusions without meaningful comment or justification.

At a minimum, the CCRB’s findings and disciplinary recommendations should command substantial deference. The NYPD should be required to address them point by point and provide a detailed public explanation for any decision to reject or weaken them.

Meaningful NYPD accountability will remain impossible until CCRB recommendations have genuine force. As long as the NYPD retains unchecked authority to disregard or dilute them, civilian oversight will remain fundamentally neutered, and systemic corruption will continue unabated.

I was struck by how well we think we can know others, and that even those closest to us - maybe especially those closest to us - can remain a mystery. I appreciated so much of this book.  I loved learning about London during this period and about how Russian money entered and influenced the city. I was/am furious how people with money seem to be untouchable- how their opportunities seem endless even as they leave destruction in their wake.

What a different perspective it gave us and the tragic family story was incredibly moving.  The book was real entry point into a side of London I was only vaguely aware of.  PRK is a terrific narrator of his own work (highly recommend Empire of Pain too for a long drive!).  I ended up truly admiring the family for sharing their trauma with a wider audience for the purpose of enlightening the rest of us to the corruption, lawlessness and violence of the oligarchy (not just in London of course).  The book was in the front display of every bookstore in London and my walks along the Thames took on a very different aspect this trip.  Thank you PRK.   People who like this book might want to watch  The Gold, a BBC crime drama series about the Brinks robbery he covers in the book.

Desertification is creeping from Africa to mediterranean Europe. Ditto Russias larger forests. 

The SW US is in a decades long drought.

Southern parts of permfrost are melting. The arctic is heating 3+ times faster than elsewhere. Growing zones are moving north... Global trends that are moving in a clear and persistent direction.

We are privileged to live within a range of ecological and environmental conditions & constraints. These are being exceeded. All our infrastructure was designed to function within certain min - max constraints, exceed design criteria and it doesn’t function adaquately.

Many people are making unwise decisions because of a lack of knowledge about coming climate change-related impacts.

People are buying houses in places that are already hot and dry, like parts of Texas and Phoenix which is one of our most rapidly growing cities. There was an article last year in this paper about how a combination of a heat wave and a power failure could send half the population of Phoenix to the hospital.

People are buying houses in places which depend on Colorado River water and in wildfire prone areas and in places like Coastal S Florida which has been experiencing more and more "sunny day flooding" as seawater backs up drains on the streets.

Roughly 10 percent of Canadian homes are now uninsurable and the number of homes in a similar predicament in the US is growing rapidly. More expensive or unavailable insurance depresses property values and when banks pull out that will be the final nail so to speak.

Impacts have been arriving sooner and with greater amplitude than expected so if you are debating when to sell your house on the coast or in the desert southwest, or some other place which you think is at elevated risk in the near future I'd say the sooner the better.

And please stop voting for climate change deniers.

When my mother passed 3 years ago leaving no will, her 7 children were left with her half-hoarded home. One lived with her at the time of her death, 2 had complicated relationships with the other 5, and 3 wanted nothing to do with settling the estate. As administrator, I had a difficult time keeping my siblings’ fingers out of the estate assets because the home was still occupied. 

The only shining ray was that Vermont’s probate court system was very helpful; doing things “by the book” and communicating every step (including legal consequences) led to the inevitable outcome that the 1 sibling moved, the house was cleared out and sold, and everyone got an equitable share of the proceeds. No “generational wealth,” but a few were able to pay off debts.

comments.body: As a real estate attorney, at least in Wisconsin, it only requires diligence to insure the transfer of title to heirs or beneficiaries. It is not as complex or fraught with complexity and cost as intimated in the article. There are online tools that allow A person to get deeds and inform yourself about title to real estate. What I have found over 40 years of practice is that problems with title transfers result from heirs procrastination, lack of diligence and coordination, and ignorance as to the process. A good real estate lawyer can untangle the spaghetti bowl pretty quickly and provide a solution. Best advice, don't sit on your hands!

comments.body:
Florida has tried to address the problem here by statute that gives certain rights to one or more of multiple claimants helping them avoid a partition suit and thereby avoid going to court. It’s too soon to judge its effectiveness. My law school alma mater created  a professor-led group consisting of 8 students to interview heirs and provide free legal aid to help clear titles to heirs property. The hope is to make establishing  the status of land titles more accessible and affordable so that the underserved can create wealth derived from fractional land ownership. 

As a long time title attorney and past president of the Florida Land Title Association  I believe more of these kinds of law school initiatives would be helpful along with making pro bono efforts by lawyers and law firms more well known in the affected communities.

comments.body: My mother transferred the historic family house, its grounds and outbuildings and 14 acres of land to a limited liability company before she died.  The LLC has 25+ members, primarily her six children’s and their children.  It has one manager, a corporation with her six children as the directors.  You would think that would make it easier to figure out what to do with the property.  But it doesn’t.  We have one of the six children’s living in it, but since she doesn’t own it, she has no incentive to invest in major renovations that the house needs.  The corporation makes management decisions, but has no really incentive to invest much in renovations either.  So, the deferred maintenance continues to add up.  There really is no easy solution to this problem.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: Unless they have a will, "many Americans" aren't leaving their property to anybody. The probate court will administer the estate and sell estate property to pay the decedent's outstanding debts. Moreover, if they do have a will, whoever is appointed to administer the estate may have to make a choice between selling estate assets to pay debts and honoring any codicil bequeathing those same assets. A common "last wishes" clause in wills includes the decedent's desire to have the estate honor their debts first before distributing what's left to heirs. Sadly, most Americans don't build "intergenerational wealth" because they die in debt and their estates must address those debts first before distributing the remaining assets. Even in cases where deeds are recorded with joint tenancy and rights of survivorship, those survivorship rights convey both property and any liens placed against it. Often, survivors must sell the property anyway to satisfy those liens because they don't have the cash to pay off the debt and keep the property. So, even having a survivor's name on the deed and being a sole inheriting heir often isn't enough to keep inherited property. Once again, Americans' problems are not lack of "wealth" per se, but too much debt.

comments.body: As long as the shows are well labeled as “parents with infants”, I’m fine with that and I’d choose not to go. But being surprised in a performance of The Odyssey or any other adult film with screaming babies, or cooing parents (or worse), is not my idea of a good time at the movies.

comments.name: Anon
comments.body:
As a childless adult, I have no problem with showings geared towards parents with children in theory, as long as they are properly advertised as such.  But I do wonder, in practice, how accommodating these cinemas truly are for patrons going to other movies who are navigating the same common areas.  I have never been to a movie theater that has enough changing tables or "family" rooms to accommodate this volume of babies, nor do I want to start or end my movie-going experience listening to babies screaming and crying in the lobby.

I also wonder--is there a cut-off age-wise for the children allowed in these showings?  An infant who can't walk is one thing, but a toddler who can squirm off a chair and start running around a dark room is a safety hazard for the child, the other patrons, and the staff.  And are the parents cleaning up after their children if they knock over food/beverages, have diaper leakage, or decide to start using the armrest/cup holder as a chewing device?  Or do they rely on minimum-wage paid staff to do that?

Perhaps we ought to have cinemas solely dedicated to the family experience.  At the very least, I'd be happy if this trend meant turning down the volume for ALL movies, which are deafening sometimes to even this 40-something's ears and brain.

comments.name: C
comments.body:
I clearly remember feeling more like a human being when I was able to go to the movies with my baby. In Portland Oregon the McMenamins owned movie theaters have offered parent friendly screenings for almost 20 years. 
I found my sanity as a new mom by bundling up my kids and heading out like a normal person to see a movie surrounded by other very relieved parents. In the slightly less darkened theater we fed out kids hummus and pita bread and relaxed into an experience that gave us at least a slice of the sense of escape and catharsis we had felt before we crossed over into the land of Baby Beluga and the Backyardigans. It felt delightful if only for a couple of hours.

Many people associate Legionnaire's disease strictly with indoor air, even though there have been a number of documented outbreaks where the people who contracted the disease were never present in the same building but had frequented the neighbourhood where the source (often a cooling tower) was located. Thanks for reporting on this as the outdoor air issue it appears to be, in this case. 

Another source of Legionnaires' disease is a home's hot water heater, when the temperature is low enough to allow the bacteria to proliferate in the heater. The exposure comes when breathing in the aerosols, say when taking a shower. This may be an important exposure route, although it won't result in outbreaks of multiple cases as reported on in the article.

If any place were ever a "commons," it is space--the place above the artificially carved out territories of the planet.  

No one owns  the skies, meaning the atmosphere--we have rules about sharing the space, among other things, to avoid crashing into one another, but also, one would have hoped, to prevent parties from fouling it.  good luck with the latter.  Certianly our country has retreated utterly from that acknowledgment of our common destiny as living beings on a shared hunk of rock and water.

We alo have treaties regarding the oceans--observed, I suppose, in the breach these days.

Low-earth orbit (LEO) is a place that elon Musk and Jeff Bezos seem to think they own, or have the right to do with as they pelase.  Ditto the inane firm that got FFC permission (for radio frequencies to control their satellites only, not ethical clearance, which the FCC does not adjudicate, or in this admin, care about) to launch lots of mirror-satellites to provide the urgently needed service of illuminating the night sky--for profit, of course.

Space is a COMMONS.  That includes the moon and Mars, Mr. Musk and Mr. Bezos and the politburo of the People's Republic of China!  

It is hard to think we are not rapidly moving down the path of self-destruction, blithely--as we sit in stupid awe of man-children with no sense of history, culture, or, obviously, basic humanity and human dignity.
